# Mythos and the Coming End of European Digital Sovereignty

(Photo by Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via AP)

Over the past years, Europe has voiced the ambition to become one of the most influential actors globally in governing artificial intelligence (AI). Through the [AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj) and the [Cyber Resilience Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act), under the rubric of digital rulemaking, Brussels engages in standard-setting that must be followed by firms and individuals.

Now, governing a technology is by no means the same as controlling the capabilities that make it powerful, and it is that gap between rule-making authority and material capacity that will decide Europe’s place in the order to come. The European Commission itself now concedes as much.

[The Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence), published on July 7, acknowledges that frontier capabilities are chiefly developed outside the European Union and that their availability is often determined by non-transparent processes, effectively positioning advanced AI as a matter of Europe’s technological sovereignty.

Europe, in other words, has understood the necessity of building and not just regulating, yet the question remains whether it can build at the speed and scale required. The recent Mythos episode is the clearest illustration of what is at stake and where the issues lie.

In the wake of a sudden and sweeping unilateral restriction on frontier artificial AI based on national security grounds by the US government, high-level meetings were scheduled at the [European Commission](https://letsdatascience.com/news/eu-commission-reviews-anthropic-export-control-consequences-2c348b30) and the [G7](https://www.reuters.com/world/tech-executives-attend-g7-summit-leaders-address-ai-online-safety-2026-06-12/) to discuss the strategic fallout of the [Mythos incident](https://www.anthropic.com/news/fable-mythos-access).

The European Commission has since urgently evaluated the practical implications of the surprising US export control directive, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has attended a G7 working lunch with world leaders to discuss the latest episode of the geopolitical securitization of AI. AI and access to certain high-capability large language models (LLMs) have become a gated strategic resource that is fenced off from those humans who reside in the wrong countries or possess the wrong passports.

When the US government issued an order suspending access to Anthropic’s Fable 5 – an LLM with guardrails that is based on the Mythos model – to foreign nationals on June 12, the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/12/technology/anthropic-mythos-fable5-blocked.html) notes that “the order limiting who can use Anthropic’s technology is unusually expansive,” and that “foreign nationals who work for Anthropic are also affected by the suspension,” which includes the firm’s recent star hire: the former OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy. This restriction offers an insight into a nascent form of frontier AI governance, which directly affects Europe’s sovereign enclosure.

The recent US government intervention involving Anthropic’s advanced AI models illustrates this emerging reality. A decision by Washington affecting access to frontier AI systems demonstrates that access to highly capable models may increasingly depend on geopolitical considerations, export controls, and national security decisions. For European policymakers, the episode raises a difficult question: What happens when the technologies shaping economic competitiveness, scientific discovery, and national security are controlled elsewhere? The answer may determine whether Europe becomes a genuine technological power in the age of AI or whether it remains primarily a rule-maker in an ecosystem shaped by others.

## Limits of AI governance

This emerging reality exposes a somewhat painful truth about the geopolitical posture of European states. Europe is in the curious situation of being structurally arranged to notice the future, regulate the future, moralize the future, and *not* be involved in building the future.

In Brussels, the EU institutions regurgitate European sovereignty, as policymakers actively construct safety standards and regulation frameworks to protect EU citizens. But in the AI domain and the endeavor to harness the technology that defines the future of humanity, sovereignty gives precedence to the ability to produce semiconductors, exponentially growing amounts of required energy, data centers, as well as to organize and attract global talent, capital, and deployment channels. Europe and its decision-makers tragically confuse rule-making capacity with future-shaping capacity in AI.

In fairness, Brussels now acknowledges this truth. The EU’s[Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence) is unusually blunt in stating that Europe must “develop its own sovereign general-purpose frontier AI capabilities to mitigate the risk of new dependencies,” and warns that “without compute, models, and data infrastructure, Europe is bound to remain a vulnerable user of frontier AI systems made elsewhere that others can suddenly switch off.”

The Commission appears to have made a 360-degree change on its previous preference to regulate while others build; it is now explicitly, too, talking about capability and infrastructure. In short, the insight is no longer contested even in Brussels, though the execution is unresolved, as it becomes questionable whether a politically fragmented EU can convert this recognition into executable steps.

A critical [scenario](https://europe2031.ai/), titled “Europe 2031,” published by a group of AI researchers just a day prior, on June 11, cautions, “unless we embark on it now, Europe will lose the ability to shape its own future,” though policymakers might utter feelings that are closer to “No more American AI; no American clouds.”

As if that is a win, and has merit all by itself. What is critical to realize in such a scenario — a partial de-risking or full decoupling from US technology — is that this represents a strategically hollow autonomy, which is fundamentally unsupported and unsustainable by material capacity and capability. EU policymakers seem to have forgotten that digital sovereignty cannot simply be legislated into existence through regulations and procurement rules. Digital sovereignty is developed over time through attracting talent that is well paid, a wide regulatory space to experiment, cheap energy, and abundant physical infrastructure like data centers.

## The material bottleneck

To understand Europe’s precarious position on AI, one must have a hard look in physical preconditions. The development of AI at rapid speeds requires continuous electricity, vast space or land, industrial cooling, cutting-edge semiconductors, optimized supply chains, and specialists who demand astronomical (for European conditions) salaries. As an [industry observer](https://christophermschroeder.substack.com/p/ai-and-geopolitics) rightly notes, “AI leadership is very much about massive financial capital, massive access to energy and GPUs, and the best world-class talent.”

While Europe has a pipeline of well-trained specialists through numerous universities and the necessary entrepreneurial spirit, too, the foundational conditions required for frontier AI are either overtly hostile or chronically undersupplied and further constrained by bureaucratic inertia. Starting with cheap and reliable power, energy in today’s Europe is mainly seen as an environmental issue that must be solved through costly and non-continuous renewables. The European Commission speaks of the need to achieve “[sustainable digitalization](https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-presents-measures-digitalise-europes-energy-system-while-ensuring-sustainable-2026-06-03_en),” while external pressures like Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz further complicate [energy security](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/energysource/conflicts-are-jolting-energy-systems-will-they-cause-structural-breaks/) in Europe.

Yet, continuous and cheap electricity is the absolute baseline of AI development. And it is required not in ten, twenty, or fifty years, but immediately. Computational capacity, critical to AI development, must scale and thus demands immediate grid access, rapid permitting processes, immense capital concentration, and speedy data-center buildouts. But anybody living in Europe today, for instance in Germany, understands well how a scaled and sustained demand for more (really, much cheaper) energy would send political factions like the Green Party spiraling, and thus, that issue alone would run into domestic party conflict and never-ending debates without resolution.

Global talent inevitably follows the highest salaries and most ambitious AI labs in order to work on meaningful and life-changing projects. But Europe’s labs remain overburdened by structural costs and regulatory constraints, as well as the formidable competition from [US-omniscalers and Chinese state-industrial mobilization](https://www.mckinsey.com/mgi/our-research/the-race-takes-off-in-the-next-big-arenas-of-competition#/). In essence, a structurally handicapped Europe is regulating AI faster than it can act on energy security or energy costs to facilitate and support an AI boom.

## The coming vassal position of Europe

These material weaknesses inherent to contemporary Europe inexorably lead to geopolitical consequences. If the US ultimately controls the best AI systems, and China commands the advanced industrial frontier, Europe will not emerge as a balancing third pole in the race to the technology of the future. What appears more likely is that European states and their populations will end up as what Axel Voss, a member of the European Parliament, called a “[digital colony](https://www.euractiv.com/news/mep-axel-voss-publishes-eu-digital-manifesto-warns-of-eus-digital-dependency/)” of other powers. As a consequence, Europe will continue to lose talent and be reduced to a consumer, regulator, and passive bargaining object. As the [scenario](https://europe2031.ai/) predicts for April 2029 (one must mention, only three years from now), “Europe depends on American AI, but the US has no such dependency on Europe.”

Economic dependence then becomes a brutal political reality because someone else possesses the power to ration access to frontier technology, right as the US becomes more transactional by the day, indicating a dangerous mixture.

For March 2031, the [scenario](https://europe2031.ai/) grimly notes, “American labs hold the cognitive frontier; China still holds the physical one. Atlas [a fictitious US firm] alone is worth more than every listed European company combined.” One has to acknowledge that in a future where European industry, defense, and scientific research are fundamentally reliant on foreign AI models, the capacity and room for independent actions and decisions will be reduced or vanish.

Europe could well face delayed or no access, country-tiered inference licensing, or the constant threat of having its most critical digital technology throttled by a third party. In such a future, any attempt of European actors to reassert geopolitical independence will be constrained and punished, since the valve to transformative AI (or other technology) is opened or closed in either the US or China. To be blunt, even if Europe aims to strike back in a tit-for-tat, it will lack reciprocal leverage, because in that asymmetrical reality, [“obvious retaliation is self-defeating,”](https://europe2031.ai/) which leaves the continent functionally subservient and weak, unable to dictate its own technological future.

Tellingly, the EU [Action Plan](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence) already anticipates this exact predicament. It instructs that a forthcoming “European Blueprint” for structured access to advanced AI shall include contingency measures for the potential situation where access to a model “is restricted or withdrawn by a provider or a third-country authority.” This, of course, is an implicit admission that a Mythos-type shut-off is not a remote hypothetical but a contingency Brussels is now formally planning around. Ironically, the fact that the Commission is drafting fallback procedures for the day the AI-valve is closed is strong evidence that the vassal position described in this article is already being priced in.

## AI as a technological multiplier

Skeptics may well argue that the risks illustrated in the scenario Europe 2031 are overblown and inflated, or viewed through the distorted lens of a US obsession with an [imagined race](https://www.transformernews.ai/p/us-china-ai-race-narrative-lobbying-openai-biden-trump?utm_medium=email) to artificial general or super intelligence (AGI/ASI). However, one does need to take the belief in an imminently arriving omnipotent technology, such as AI, to recognize the universal gravity of Europe’s strategic positioning.

The argument is broader and holds even if AI never achieves the most extreme forecasts of sentience or capabilities beyond what humans can do. As many recognize, AI already proves to radically increase human productivity and advance scientific discovery across most disciplines, such as fundamental science, cyber defense, and advanced robotics, proving its value as a [technological multiplier](https://www.cnas.org/publications/reports/artificial-intelligence-and-international-security) in this early phase of AI development.

Europe’s dependence on the US and China can easily become critical even without AI becoming omnipotent. Crucially, missing the foundations of this technological era means Europe operating at a persistent structural disadvantage in every subsequent arena of global competition, risking permanently bogging down Europe in scientific innovation and making it perpetually vulnerable in defense.

The most tragic aspect of the current trajectory is that the result will not stem from ignorance; the impending crisis is widely understood. But European politics appears to be simply unable to metabolize the writing on the wall. The [required corrections](https://x.com/s8mb/status/2065715249303507048) to set Europe up for success – continuous and cheap electricity, rapid grid connections, permissive data-center zoning, massive capital concentration – are too monumental and structural for a politically disunited Europe to undertake in time.

All that becomes clearer as wartime-speed industrial modernization due to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, even under European unity, has proven insufficient. Vetoing and regulating is the new mantra of European modernization. If nothing fundamental changes in the coming years, historians will note the narrative failure, as predicted for [June 2034 in the scenario](https://europe2031.ai/): “We had a negative vision. We were good at negative visions. (…) The political environment is never ready.” The ultimate indictment might be the realization that “there was a chance and we did not even try.”

Europe’s future is not likely to be decided by military subjugation or other external events; it will much more likely be strongly influenced by AI-linked conditions imposed by third parties, such as conditional licensing, rationing, API-gating, and high prices, with little to no pathways of resistance. Europe’s future might be placed behind a gate that itself no longer controls.

## What European success in AI would look like

If diagnosis were the measure of success, Europe would already have won; as a German proverb states, “we do not have a knowledge problem, only an implementation problem.” Europe and its institutions know what the issue is, and success does not require Europe to out-build the US or out-manufacture China. It requires something simple to state and hard to obtain: enough sovereign capability so that access to frontier AI cannot be switched off from the outside without a European fallback ready to soften the blow.

Concretely, this means treating the obviously ambitious commitments in the [EU Action Plan](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence) as obligations. The EU Commission concedes that building Europe’s frontier capacity “will entail hundreds of billions of euro investment needs which can only be partly covered by public finances” and that although “the cost for Europe of building its own frontier AI capacity may be very large, the cost of not building it may be even larger and grow every year as the AI-capability gap widens.” Thus, private capital would be necessary to close funding gaps.

Nevertheless, execution on the unglamorous foundations described above, such as rapid grid connections, quick permits, fewer regulations, and most critically, cheap energy, remains undisputed. Encouraging, the mentioned “European Blueprint” of structured access is certainly worth pursuing, but it can only be a supplement to sovereign capacity. A fallback plan for having ones AI-valve turned off by outside parties cannot be equated to being un-switch-off-able, which really should be Europe’s ultimate long-term objective. A minimum requirement for European success in AI would be resilience due to the ability to weather a Mythos-styled restriction without European industry, defense, and research grinding to a halt.

Whether Europe and its institutions in Brussels are able to create suitable conditions for success in AI, however, is not decided by the quality of analysis, for instance, in the EU Action Plan, but by political will to encourage and sustain the building of indigenous AI in Europe.

歐洲委員會隨後緊急評估了美國這項出人意料出口管制指令的實際影響，同時 Anthropic 執行長 Dario Amodei 參加了一場與世界領導人的 G7 工作午餐，討論 AI 地緣政治安全化的最新進展。AI 以及某些高能力大型語言模型（LLM）的使用權已成為受管制的戰略資源，被隔離給那些居住在「不對的國家」或持有「不對護照」的人。

美國政府在 6 月 12 日頒布命令，禁止外國籍人士使用 Anthropic 的 Fable 5 — 一款基於 Mythos 模型、具有防護機制的大型語言模型。根據《紐約時報》的報導，這項命令「限制誰可以使用 Anthropic 技術的範圍異常廣泛」，且「在 Anthropic 工作的外國籍人士也受到禁令影響」，包括該公司最近聘僱的明星員工、OpenAI 前共同創辦人 Andrej Karpathy。這項限制措施讓我們得以窺見一種新興的邊境 AI 治理形態，這直接影響歐洲的主權領地。

美國政府最近涉及 Anthropic 先進 AI 模型的干預說明了這一新興現實。華盛頓的一項決定影響到對邊境 AI 系統的使用權，表明對高能力模型的存取可能日益受地緣政治考量、出口管制和國家安全決策所制約。對歐洲政策制定者而言，這一事件提出了一個棘手的問題：當塑造經濟競爭力、科學發現和國家安全的技術被他人控制時會發生什麼？答案可能決定歐洲是否會成為 AI 時代的真正技術大國，還是只能在由他人塑造的生態系統中扮演規則制定者的角色。

## AI 治理的限度

這一新興現實暴露了一個多少令人痛楚的真相，關乎歐洲國家的地緣政治態勢。歐洲處於一個奇異的局面：結構上被安排去觀察未來、規管未來、道德判斷未來，卻*沒有*參與建構未來。

在布魯塞爾，歐盟機構高喊歐洲主權，政策制定者積極建構安全標準與監管框架以保護歐盟公民。但在 AI 領域及掌握定義人類未來之技術的努力上，主權取決於能否生產半導體、積累所需龐大能源與數據中心、組織並吸引全球人才、資本與部署管道的能力。歐洲及其決策者悲劇地把制定規則的能力混淆為塑造未來的能力。

公道地說，布魯塞爾現已認識到這一事實。歐盟的[《網路安全與人工智慧行動計畫》](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence)在陳述歐洲必須「開發自主的通用前沿 AI 能力以降低新依賴風險」時出奇地直言，並警告「沒有計算資源、模型與數據基礎設施，歐洲勢必只能成為他人製造的前沿 AI 系統的脆弱使用者，而他人隨時可能關閉這些系統」。

歐委會看似在「邊規管邊讓他人建設」的前任偏好上做了 180度轉變；如今它也在明確地談論能力與基礎設施。簡言之，這一洞見在布魯塞爾已不再有爭議，但執行面仍未定案，因為政治上分裂的歐盟是否能把這一認知轉化為可執行的步驟變得令人質疑。

由 AI 研究人員發表、標題為「2031 年歐洲」的關鍵[情景分析](https://europe2031.ai/)在 6 月 11 日發布，警告「除非我們現在著手進行，否則歐洲將失去塑造自身未來的能力」，儘管政策制定者可能會吐露更接近「不要美國 AI；不要美國雲端」的想法。

彷彿這就是勝利，本身就有價值。在這種情況下——無論是部分降低對美國科技的風險或完全脫鉤——關鍵是要認識到，這代表的是一種戰略上空洞的自主性，根本上缺乏物質與技術能力的支撐，且無法永續維持。歐盟政策制定者似乎忘記了數位主權無法單純透過法規和採購規則就創造出來。數位主權是透過時間發展而來的，需要吸引高薪人才、充分的監管實驗空間、廉價能源，以及如資料中心等充足的實體基礎設施。

## 物質瓶頸

要理解歐洲在 AI 上的危險處境，必須認真審視物質前提條件。AI 快速發展需要持續供電、廣大的空間或土地、工業級冷卻、尖端半導體、最佳化的供應鏈，以及要求天文數字級薪酬（按歐洲標準）的專家。如一位[業界觀察者](https://christophermschroeder.substack.com/p/ai-and-geopolitics)所言，「AI 領導力主要取決於龐大的金融資本、廣泛的能源和 GPU 取得管道，以及最頂級的世界人才。」

雖然歐洲透過眾多大學擁有訓練充分的專家隊伍，也具備必要的創業精神，但前沿 AI 所需的基礎條件要不是公然不利，要不就是長期供應不足，而且受官僚惰性進一步束縛。從廉價可靠的電力開始，當今歐洲的能源主要被視為環保議題，必須透過成本高昂且間歇性的再生能源來解決。歐盟執委會提及達成「[永續數位化](https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-presents-measures-digitalise-europes-energy-system-while-ensuring-sustainable-2026-06-03_en)」的必要性，而俄烏戰爭和荷莫茲海峽封鎖等外部壓力進一步加劇歐洲的[能源安全](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/energysource/conflicts-are-jolting-energy-systems-will-they-cause-structural-breaks/)問題。

然而，穩定廉價的電力是AI開發的絕對基礎。這不是十年、二十年或五十年後的事，而是現在立刻就需要。運算能力對AI開發至關重要，必須擴大規模，因此需要立即的電網連接、快速核准、巨額資本投入，以及迅速的資料中心擴建。但任何現在住在歐洲的人，比如德國，都能充分理解，對更多（實際上便宜得多）能源的規模化、持續性需求，會如何讓綠黨（Green Party）等政治派系陷入困境，因此，這個議題單獨就會引發國內政黨衝突和沒完沒了的爭論。

## 歐洲迫在眼前的附庸地位

歐洲內在的這些實質性弱點，必然導致地緣政治後果。若美國最終掌控最優質的AI系統，中國主宰先進工業前沿，歐洲將無法成為未來科技競賽中的平衡第三極。更有可能的情形是，歐洲國家及其人民最終會淪為歐洲議會議員Axel Voss所稱其他勢力的「[數位殖民地](https://www.euractiv.com/news/mep-axel-voss-publishes-eu-digital-manifesto-warns-of-eus-digital-dependency/)」。因此，歐洲將持續失去人才，淪為消費者、監管者和被動的談判籌碼。如[預測情景](https://europe2031.ai/)針對2029年4月的預測（得提一下，距今僅三年），「歐洲依賴美國AI，但美國對歐洲沒有此種依賴」。

經濟依賴因此成為殘酷的政治現實，因為他人掌控著限制前沿科技可及性的權力，而美國日趨交易化，形成危險的混合。

針對 2031 年 3 月，[情景](https://europe2031.ai/)沉重地指出：「美國實驗室掌控認知領域的前沿；中國仍掌控實體領域。虛構美企 Atlas 單獨的價值就超過所有上市歐洲公司的總和。」必須承認，在未來若歐洲產業、國防與科學研究根本上依賴外國 AI 模型，獨立行動與決策的空間與能力將縮減或消失。

歐洲很可能面臨延遲或無法取得、按國家分級的推理授權，或被第三方隨時卡住最關鍵數位科技的威脅。在這樣的未來，歐洲行為者任何重申地緣政治獨立的嘗試都將受限與遭懲罰，因為變革性 AI（或其他技術）的閥門掌握在美國或中國手中。坦白說，即使歐洲想以牙還牙，也缺乏相等的籌碼，因為在這種不對稱的現實中，[「顯而易見的報復自取其辱」](https://europe2031.ai/)，使歐洲實質上屈從於人且虛弱，無法掌控自己的科技未來。

值得注意的是，歐盟 [Action Plan](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence) 已預見此困境。它指示未來的「歐洲藍圖」應包含應急措施，以應對進階 AI 模型的取得可能被「供應商或第三國當局限制或撤銷」的情況。當然，這隱含地承認，Mythos 式的斷電並非遠方的假想，而是布魯塞爾目前正式規劃的應變。諷刺的是，執委會正在制定 AI 閥門關閉之日的備用程序這一事實，強烈證明了本文所描述的附庸地位已被納入計價。

## AI 作為科技倍增器

懷疑者可能會主張《2031年歐洲情景》所示的風險被誇大了，或者透過美國對於達成人工通用智能或超智能（AGI/ASI）的[想像的競賽](https://www.transformernews.ai/p/us-china-ai-race-narrative-lobbying-openai-biden-trump?utm_medium=email)的扭曲視角來看待。然而，人們只需要相信一項迫在眉睫的全能科技（如AI）即將到來，就足以認識到歐洲戰略定位的普遍重要性。

這個論點範圍更廣——即使AI永遠無法達到對有意識或超越人類能力的最極端預測，這個論點仍然成立。正如許多人所認識到的，AI已經證明能夠大幅提升人類生產力，推進基礎科學、網路防禦和進階機器人學等大多數學科的科學發現，在AI發展的這個早期階段證明了它作為[技術倍增器](https://www.cnas.org/publications/reports/artificial-intelligence-and-international-security)的價值。

歐洲對美國和中國的依賴即使在AI不成為全能科技的情況下，也很容易變成關鍵問題。關鍵是，錯失這個科技時代的基礎，意味著歐洲在全球競爭的每一個後續領域都面臨持續的結構性劣勢，面臨永久性地在科學創新上陷入困頓，並在國防上永遠脆弱的風險。

目前軌跡最悲劇的一面是結果將不是源於無知；迫在眉睫的危機已廣為人知。但歐洲政治似乎根本無法正視這些警訊。要讓歐洲成功所[需的改正](https://x.com/s8mb/status/2065715249303507048)——穩定廉價的電力供應、快速的電網連接、寬鬆的資料中心區劃、大規模的資本集中——對政治上不統一的歐洲來說太龐大且結構性了，無法及時實施。

隨著俄烏全面戰爭導致的戰時速度工業現代化在歐洲團結下仍證明不足，這一切變得更加清晰。否決與監管成為歐洲現代化的新方針。如果未來幾年沒有根本改變，歷史學家將記錄這場敘事失敗，正如 [該情景對 2034 年 6 月的預測](https://europe2031.ai/)：「我們有消極願景。我們很擅長負面願景。（...）政治環境永遠還沒準備好。」終極的控訴可能是意識到「機會擺在面前，我們甚至沒有試過。」

歐洲的未來不太可能由軍事征服或其他外部事件決定；更可能是被第三方施加的 AI 相關條件強烈影響，例如有條件授權、配給制、API 限制與高價格，幾乎沒有任何抵抗途徑。歐洲的未來可能被置於一扇它自己不再控制的門後。

## 歐洲在 AI 上的成功會是什麼樣子

如果診斷是衡量成功的標準，歐洲早就贏了；正如一句德國諺語所說，「我們沒有知識問題，只有執行問題。」歐洲及其機構清楚問題所在，成功不需要歐洲建造能力超過美國、製造能力超過中國。它需要的是簡單易述卻難以實現的東西：足夠的自主能力，使得即使對前沿 AI 的存取被外部切斷，歐洲也有準備好的替代方案來減輕衝擊。

具體來說，這意味著把 [歐盟行動計畫](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence) 中那些明顯雄心勃勃的承諾當作義務來對待。歐盟委員會承認，建設歐洲的前沿能力「將需要數千億歐元投資，這些投資只能由公共財政部分承擔」，並指出雖然「歐洲建設自己的前沿 AI 能力的成本可能非常龐大，但不建設的成本可能更大，並且隨著 AI 能力差距擴大而逐年增加。」因此，需要私人資本來彌補資金缺口。

儘管如此，上述那些看似平凡但根本性的執行基礎——例如迅速的電網接入、快速的許可審批、減少法規限制，以及最關鍵的廉價能源——仍然是無可爭議的必要條件。令人鼓舞的是，所提到的「歐洲藍圖」（結構化准入）確實值得追求，但它只能補充主權能力。應對人工智能開關被外部方關閉的備用計畫，不能等同於根本無法被關閉的能力——歐洲真正的終極長期目標應該是後者。歐洲在人工智能上成功的最低要求是具備韌性，在面臨 Mythos 式的限制時，仍能保持產業、國防和研究不致癱瘓。

然而，歐洲及其布魯塞爾機構能否為人工智能的成功創造適當條件，並不取決於分析品質（例如歐盟行動計畫中的分析），而是取決於推進和維持歐洲本土人工智能發展的政治意志。

當代歐洲固有的這些材料弱點最終會帶來地緣政治後果。如果美國最終掌握最佳的人工智慧系統，而中國則主導先進工業的前沿，那麼歐洲就無法在未來的科技競賽中扮演平衡第三極的角色。更可能的情況是，歐洲各國及其人民將淪為其他強權的「[數位殖民地](https://www.euractiv.com/news/mep-axel-voss-publishes-eu-digital-manifesto-warns-of-eus-digital-dependency/)」。

歐委會看似在「邊規管邊讓他人建設」的前任偏好上做了 180度轉變；如今它也在明確地談論能力與基礎設施。簡言之，這一洞見在布魯塞爾已不再有爭議，但執行面仍未定案，因為政治上分裂的歐盟是否能把這一認知轉化為可執行的步驟變得令人質疑。

由 AI 研究人員發表、標題為「2031 年歐洲」的關鍵[情景分析](https://europe2031.ai/)在 6 月 11 日發布，警告「除非我們現在著手進行，否則歐洲將失去塑造自身未來的能力」，儘管政策制定者可能會吐露更接近「不要美國 AI；不要美國雲端」的想法。

彷彿這就是勝利，本身就有價值。在這種情況下——無論是部分降低對美國科技的風險或完全脫鉤——關鍵是要認識到，這代表的是一種戰略上空洞的自主性，根本上缺乏物質與技術能力的支撐，且無法永續維持。歐盟政策制定者似乎忘記了數位主權無法單純透過法規和採購規則就創造出來。數位主權是透過時間發展而來的，需要吸引高薪人才、充分的監管實驗空間、廉價能源，以及如資料中心等充足的實體基礎設施。

## 物質瓶頸

要理解歐洲在 AI 上的危險處境，必須認真審視物質前提條件。AI 快速發展需要持續供電、廣大的空間或土地、工業級冷卻、尖端半導體、最佳化的供應鏈，以及要求天文數字級薪酬（按歐洲標準）的專家。如一位[業界觀察者](https://christophermschroeder.substack.com/p/ai-and-geopolitics)所言，「AI 領導力主要取決於龐大的金融資本、廣泛的能源和 GPU 取得管道，以及最頂級的世界人才。」

雖然歐洲透過眾多大學擁有訓練充分的專家隊伍，也具備必要的創業精神，但前沿 AI 所需的基礎條件要不是公然不利，要不就是長期供應不足，而且受官僚惰性進一步束縛。從廉價可靠的電力開始，當今歐洲的能源主要被視為環保議題，必須透過成本高昂且間歇性的再生能源來解決。歐盟執委會提及達成「[永續數位化](https://energy.ec.europa.eu/news/commission-presents-measures-digitalise-europes-energy-system-while-ensuring-sustainable-2026-06-03_en)」的必要性，而俄烏戰爭和荷莫茲海峽封鎖等外部壓力進一步加劇歐洲的[能源安全](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/energysource/conflicts-are-jolting-energy-systems-will-they-cause-structural-breaks/)問題。

然而，穩定廉價的電力是AI開發的絕對基礎。這不是十年、二十年或五十年後的事，而是現在立刻就需要。運算能力對AI開發至關重要，必須擴大規模，因此需要立即的電網連接、快速核准、巨額資本投入，以及迅速的資料中心擴建。但任何現在住在歐洲的人，比如德國，都能充分理解，對更多（實際上便宜得多）能源的規模化、持續性需求，會如何讓綠黨（Green Party）等政治派系陷入困境，因此，這個議題單獨就會引發國內政黨衝突和沒完沒了的爭論。

## 歐洲迫在眼前的附庸地位

歐洲內在的這些實質性弱點，必然導致地緣政治後果。若美國最終掌控最優質的AI系統，中國主宰先進工業前沿，歐洲將無法成為未來科技競賽中的平衡第三極。更有可能的情形是，歐洲國家及其人民最終會淪為歐洲議會議員Axel Voss所稱其他勢力的「[數位殖民地](https://www.euractiv.com/news/mep-axel-voss-publishes-eu-digital-manifesto-warns-of-eus-digital-dependency/)」。因此，歐洲將持續失去人才，淪為消費者、監管者和被動的談判籌碼。如[預測情景](https://europe2031.ai/)針對2029年4月的預測（得提一下，距今僅三年），「歐洲依賴美國AI，但美國對歐洲沒有此種依賴」。

經濟依賴因此成為殘酷的政治現實，因為他人掌控著限制前沿科技可及性的權力，而美國日趨交易化，形成危險的混合。

針對 2031 年 3 月，[情景](https://europe2031.ai/)沉重地指出：「美國實驗室掌控認知領域的前沿；中國仍掌控實體領域。虛構美企 Atlas 單獨的價值就超過所有上市歐洲公司的總和。」必須承認，在未來若歐洲產業、國防與科學研究根本上依賴外國 AI 模型，獨立行動與決策的空間與能力將縮減或消失。

歐洲很可能面臨延遲或無法取得、按國家分級的推理授權，或被第三方隨時卡住最關鍵數位科技的威脅。在這樣的未來，歐洲行為者任何重申地緣政治獨立的嘗試都將受限與遭懲罰，因為變革性 AI（或其他技術）的閥門掌握在美國或中國手中。坦白說，即使歐洲想以牙還牙，也缺乏相等的籌碼，因為在這種不對稱的現實中，[「顯而易見的報復自取其辱」](https://europe2031.ai/)，使歐洲實質上屈從於人且虛弱，無法掌控自己的科技未來。

值得注意的是，歐盟 [Action Plan](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence) 已預見此困境。它指示未來的「歐洲藍圖」應包含應急措施，以應對進階 AI 模型的取得可能被「供應商或第三國當局限制或撤銷」的情況。當然，這隱含地承認，Mythos 式的斷電並非遠方的假想，而是布魯塞爾目前正式規劃的應變。諷刺的是，執委會正在制定 AI 閥門關閉之日的備用程序這一事實，強烈證明了本文所描述的附庸地位已被納入計價。

## AI 作為科技倍增器

懷疑者可能會主張《2031年歐洲情景》所示的風險被誇大了，或者透過美國對於達成人工通用智能或超智能（AGI/ASI）的[想像的競賽](https://www.transformernews.ai/p/us-china-ai-race-narrative-lobbying-openai-biden-trump?utm_medium=email)的扭曲視角來看待。然而，人們只需要相信一項迫在眉睫的全能科技（如AI）即將到來，就足以認識到歐洲戰略定位的普遍重要性。

這個論點範圍更廣——即使AI永遠無法達到對有意識或超越人類能力的最極端預測，這個論點仍然成立。正如許多人所認識到的，AI已經證明能夠大幅提升人類生產力，推進基礎科學、網路防禦和進階機器人學等大多數學科的科學發現，在AI發展的這個早期階段證明了它作為[技術倍增器](https://www.cnas.org/publications/reports/artificial-intelligence-and-international-security)的價值。

歐洲對美國和中國的依賴即使在AI不成為全能科技的情況下，也很容易變成關鍵問題。關鍵是，錯失這個科技時代的基礎，意味著歐洲在全球競爭的每一個後續領域都面臨持續的結構性劣勢，面臨永久性地在科學創新上陷入困頓，並在國防上永遠脆弱的風險。

目前軌跡最悲劇的一面是結果將不是源於無知；迫在眉睫的危機已廣為人知。但歐洲政治似乎根本無法正視這些警訊。要讓歐洲成功所[需的改正](https://x.com/s8mb/status/2065715249303507048)——穩定廉價的電力供應、快速的電網連接、寬鬆的資料中心區劃、大規模的資本集中——對政治上不統一的歐洲來說太龐大且結構性了，無法及時實施。

隨著俄烏全面戰爭導致的戰時速度工業現代化在歐洲團結下仍證明不足，這一切變得更加清晰。否決與監管成為歐洲現代化的新方針。如果未來幾年沒有根本改變，歷史學家將記錄這場敘事失敗，正如 [該情景對 2034 年 6 月的預測](https://europe2031.ai/)：「我們有消極願景。我們很擅長負面願景。（...）政治環境永遠還沒準備好。」終極的控訴可能是意識到「機會擺在面前，我們甚至沒有試過。」

歐洲的未來不太可能由軍事征服或其他外部事件決定；更可能是被第三方施加的 AI 相關條件強烈影響，例如有條件授權、配給制、API 限制與高價格，幾乎沒有任何抵抗途徑。歐洲的未來可能被置於一扇它自己不再控制的門後。

## 歐洲在 AI 上的成功會是什麼樣子

如果診斷是衡量成功的標準，歐洲早就贏了；正如一句德國諺語所說，「我們沒有知識問題，只有執行問題。」歐洲及其機構清楚問題所在，成功不需要歐洲建造能力超過美國、製造能力超過中國。它需要的是簡單易述卻難以實現的東西：足夠的自主能力，使得即使對前沿 AI 的存取被外部切斷，歐洲也有準備好的替代方案來減輕衝擊。

具體來說，這意味著把 [歐盟行動計畫](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-action-plan-cybersecurity-and-artificial-intelligence) 中那些明顯雄心勃勃的承諾當作義務來對待。歐盟委員會承認，建設歐洲的前沿能力「將需要數千億歐元投資，這些投資只能由公共財政部分承擔」，並指出雖然「歐洲建設自己的前沿 AI 能力的成本可能非常龐大，但不建設的成本可能更大，並且隨著 AI 能力差距擴大而逐年增加。」因此，需要私人資本來彌補資金缺口。

儘管如此，上述那些看似平凡但根本性的執行基礎——例如迅速的電網接入、快速的許可審批、減少法規限制，以及最關鍵的廉價能源——仍然是無可爭議的必要條件。令人鼓舞的是，所提到的「歐洲藍圖」（結構化准入）確實值得追求，但它只能補充主權能力。應對人工智能開關被外部方關閉的備用計畫，不能等同於根本無法被關閉的能力——歐洲真正的終極長期目標應該是後者。歐洲在人工智能上成功的最低要求是具備韌性，在面臨 Mythos 式的限制時，仍能保持產業、國防和研究不致癱瘓。

然而，歐洲及其布魯塞爾機構能否為人工智能的成功創造適當條件，並不取決於分析品質（例如歐盟行動計畫中的分析），而是取決於推進和維持歐洲本土人工智能發展的政治意志。
